tutorial.title: How budgets work
tutorial.intro: Budgets let you cap how much you spend on a category during a given month, and see live how close you are to that cap.

s1.heading: 1. Set a limit per category
s1.body: Pick a category, a month and year, and how much you want to spend at most on it during that period.

s2.heading: 2. Watch it fill up automatically
s2.body: Every expense you log against that category counts toward the limit — there is nothing else to do. The progress bar and the spent/remaining numbers update on their own.

s3.heading: 3. Colors tell you the status
s3.body: Green (OK) while you are under 80% spent, amber (Warning) from 80% up, red (Exceeded) once you go over the limit.

s4.heading: 4. Budgets are per month
s4.body: Switch the month/year selector at the top to review a past period or set up next month's limits ahead of time.

tutorial.title: How recurring transactions work
tutorial.intro: Recurring transactions are templates for movements that happen on a schedule — rent, a subscription, your salary — so you don't have to enter them by hand every time.

s1.heading: 1. Create a template
s1.body: A template is a transaction blueprint: amount, account, category (or destination account for transfers), counterparty and how often it repeats.

s2.heading: 2. Nothing fires by itself — yet
s2.body: There is no background job running in this app. A template only turns into a real transaction when you press "Run" on it, or when someone calls the run-due endpoint (meant for an external scheduler).

s3.heading: 3. Run now vs. next run date
s3.body: "Run" generates one occurrence immediately, regardless of the scheduled date, and advances the template's cursor. The "Next run" column shows when it would fire on its own once a scheduler exists.

s4.heading: 4. Pause instead of deleting
s4.body: Turn a template inactive to stop it from counting as due without losing its configuration — useful for a subscription you paused, for example.

tutorial.title: How savings goals work
tutorial.intro: Savings goals let you set real money aside for something specific. What you add to a goal leaves your regular balance and is tracked under Savings until you take it back.

s1.heading: 1. Name a target
s1.body: Give the goal a name, an icon, how much you need to reach it, and the date you want to reach it by.

s2.heading: 2. Set money aside
s2.body: Use "Add money" to move an amount from one of your accounts into the goal. That money leaves your regular balance and shows up under Savings instead — it is really set aside. "Withdraw" brings some of it back whenever you need it.

s3.heading: 3. Progress is calculated for you
s3.body: Progress %, remaining amount, monthly amount required and days left all derive from what the goal holds and its target date. The optional linked account is just the default source when you add money.

s4.heading: 4. When the date arrives
s4.body: Nothing moves on its own. A goal shows "Achieved" once it holds the target, or "Overdue" if the date passed first. Either way you decide: extend the date, keep adding, or "Close" it to send everything back to an account.
